title: What jazz means, and swing versus jazz
summary: She discusses being called a jazz singer, that swing replaced jazz, ragtime versus jazz, and the 'jazz' label Duke Ellington disliked.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well, according to all the conversations we've been having all day, you certainly have to be classified as a community activist as well and a very lively politician, not in a derogatory sense, a political activist.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Someone was saying, how did I feel about being called a jazz singer because I wasn't called a jazz singer in the beginning. Of course, my answer to that is that in 1937 jazz, you know, as an expression was considered passe and I actually came in on the swing era, so I guess --
The notion was that swing had replaced jazz.

Yes, and -- yeah, it's not funny, you know, when you consider -- well, swing definitely had to do with the big bands and jazz was always a small thing. I mean when you get over five pieces, you know, and it's swing because then you're involved in arrangements where in jazz -- the traditional jazz material, it's not arranged, but every man knows what part he's supposed to play and all that. But swing had to do with the big band arrangements, you know, and arrangements like Fletcher Henderson and Jimmy Mundy and a lot of the others, and they had the beat, it was danceable music whereas the early jazz was more or less in a march tempo, you know.
In New Orleans, certainly.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Yeh, yeh -- and swing, well, you had the Lindy Hoppers and all that.
End of Side A of Tape 5
I just have two footnotes to add: 1. The population of Sweden is not 800,000, it's about 8,000,000. 2. Charlotte is in North Carolina, not in South Carolina.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Beginning of Side B - Tape 5

Yeh, I've been trying to discover what the real distinction was between jazz and swing that made it so necessary to put down the term "jazz." I feel that I understand traditional jazz pretty well and I understand swing pretty well. Unless perhaps during the swing era the music was more danceable and the Lindy Hoppers, it was a young people's music and not necessarily traditional. It was new and it caught on.

Of course today it's very difficulty, you have to say traditional jazz or modern jazz or swing because now everything is considered jazz. If it's Bop, it's jazz. Whatever the new thing is, it's jazz, except for the latest trend, which is disco which definitely means "dance to records." And then of course there's the Hustle, that has to do with the dance.

Basically, so far as I'm concerned, the thing that identifies jazz mainly is the beat and the harmonic progression. A lot of people say the syncopation is one of the identifiable facets of jazz but you can improvise and still it doesn't have
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Sure, or some people might say that Ragtime wasn't jazz --

No, well, Ragtime was strictly limited to the pianists. You know, bands weren't -- well, I don't know -- "Alexander's Ragtime Band." But I think Ragtime definitely identified the style of piano playing, you know, not necessarily --
I suppose Jelly Roll Morton comes closest to kind of straddling the two things.
That's right.
Not in his piano playing, but in his group "The Red Hot Peppers."
Right.

What do you say to people then who don't want to use the label "jazz?" Duke Ellington didn't want to be known as a jazz musician. And lots of people now talk about Afro-American classical music and a lot of terms like that.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

I never was against the term "jazz." Jazz was jazz and swing was swing. I never got to the point where I would put down jazz because some of the early music that was considered jazz that was the kind of music that I liked. So there's no way I could put it down, you know, as a form of music that I wouldn't want to be identified with.

Of course the stories that go along with jazz, how it originated, where it originated and all that, you know, in Storyville and all that kind of stuff, well thats -- perhaps that's the only place where we could hear it because that was the only place where they could afford a piano or something like that and the musicians were attracted by the sounds that they heard from these houses and they could get in there and, you know, and play.

And then of course the traditional New Orleans jazz which supposedly originated -- came from the funerals and then coming back from the funeral -- these groups grew out of the marching bands of course because they were all the brass instruments and things
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

like that. But I like to feel that there are certain areas where the one thing evolves into the other. I believe that swing was definitely evolved from jazz. No doubt about it. Even the Bop, you know, evolved out of swing because there are musicians that hear or feel something that is not being expressed at the time. They want to stretch out a little bit. Say, for instance I would say that the -- although Dizzy Gillespie is identified with the Bop era but that's a term, you know, but I think the greatest influence on the music so far as it evolving from swing to whatever was next, was Charlie Parker who with his ideas, his approach to harmonic progressions and all, I really believe that he continued it more so than Dizzy because Charlie Parker, he played music, it was not a gimmick. I mean --
